title: The Bandgap Principle
intro: A reference voltage that does not move with supply or temperature underlies every data converter and regulator.

blocks.text: A resistor-divider reference simply follows the supply. Making a current independent of the supply is done with a self-biased circuit: a mirror that is biased from its own output, or a mirror loop where the current is set by a resistor and a transistor. Such loops have two stable states (zero current is stable too) and need a startup circuit.

items: A base-emitter voltage VBE is complementary to absolute temperature (CTAT): about -1.5 mV/K at 300 K.
The difference of two VBEs at different current densities, Delta-VBE = VT * ln(n), is proportional to absolute temperature (PTAT): about +0.086 mV/K per unit of ln(n), so for n = 8 about +0.18 mV/K.
Adding a suitable multiple m of the PTAT term to the CTAT term cancels the first-order temperature coefficient. The sum is close to the silicon bandgap voltage, about 1.2 V, hence the name.

blocks.source:
VREF = VBE + m * VT * ln(n)
Zero first-order TC when  m * ln(n) * (k/q) = 1.5 mV/K   -->  m * ln(n) about 17.4
For n = 8:  m about 8.4,   VREF about 1.2 V

blocks.text: Drag the multiplier: below about 8.4 the sum falls with temperature, above it rises; at the right value the curve is flat and only a small second-order bow remains (the real VBE has curvature that this straight-line model omits).

items: Speed and noise: the op amp that forces equal collector voltages adds offset and noise, multiplied by m. Larger bias currents and filtering help.
Low-voltage bandgaps: summing currents instead of voltages gives references below 1 V.
Curvature compensation and trimming reach ppm/K drifts.

blocks.title: PTAT voltage
blocks.text: For n = 8 and T = 300 K, find Delta-VBE = VT * ln(n). (VT = 25.85 mV.)
solution: Its temperature slope is 53.7 mV/300 K = 0.179 mV/K.

blocks.title: Cancelling the drift
blocks.text: VBE falls 1.5 mV/K. How large must m be, with n = 8, to cancel it? What is VREF if VBE = 0.75 V at 300 K?
